name: Harley-Davidson, Inc.

profile.description: Harley-Davidson designs, manufactures and sells heavyweight motorcycles, parts, accessories and apparel through its Harley-Davidson Motor Company (HDMC) segment. It also provides retail and wholesale financing through Harley-Davidson Financial Services (HDFS), in which it sold a $5B loan-book stake to KKR and PIMCO in 2025 while retaining control, and holds a majority stake in the electric-motorcycle company LiveWire Group (LVWR). CEO Artie Starrs, formerly CEO of Topgolf, took over in 2025 and launched the 'Back to the Bricks' dealer-health strategy. In Q3 2026 North American retail rose 9%, global dealer inventory fell 26%, and the company raised HDMC and HDFS guidance for the second time this year.

innovation.label: WEAK
innovation.analysis: Track Record (1/3): Harley's main new venture of the past five years is LiveWire, which remains loss-making with a 2026 operating loss guide of $70-80M, and analysts describe the new 'Back to the Bricks' plan as a return to basics rather than a reinvention [2][3]. AI Deployment (0/2): No AI products or quantified AI savings were found in research [3]. Market Share (1/2): Harley is an iconic heavyweight brand, and North American retail grew 9% in Q3 2026 for a fourth straight quarter of growth, but HDMC shipments fell 8% to 33,616 units and no share-gain data was found [1]. Pipeline (1/2): New lower-priced models such as the Super Glide, Deadwood and Low Bob are named, but launch-level revenue visibility is limited [1][3]. R&D Intensity (0/1): Harley does not break out R&D in the reported income statement, so above-average intensity cannot be shown [5].

inspiration.label: DEVELOPING
inspiration.analysis: Mission Floor (3/4): Harley's purpose of standing for 'the timeless pursuit of adventure' and freedom is specific, and the brand has expressed it for more than 120 years; few brands are so closely tied to an identity customers tattoo on themselves. Community Impact (1/2): Harley runs general corporate philanthropy through its foundation, but no distinctive dollar-quantified program was found in research. Employee Retention (0/2): No retention data was found; the 2025 CEO transition and the 2024 DEI reversal under boycott pressure point to an unsettled workforce [3][4]. Insider Buying (1/2): FMP shows three open-market purchases in each of Q1 2026 and Q3 2026 against two and three sales respectively, a roughly balanced to slightly positive pattern [6].

infrastructure.label: STRONG
infrastructure.analysis: Mechanically scored on the Dividend weighting (12 weight units). Strengths: D/E improved to 76.7% after the $5B HDFS loan-book sale was used partly to repay $450M of debt, the forward P/E is 15.6x, the payout ratio is 40.4%, dividends have been paid for 33 consecutive years, and the five-year dividend CAGR is 10.4% ($0.44 in 2020 to $0.72 in 2025) [4][5]. Weaknesses: TTM ROE (-4.2%) and profit margin (-3.3%) are negative, revenue fell 19.2% YoY, the five-year revenue CAGR is only 2.0% ($4.05B to $4.47B), and dividend growth runs only five years after the 2020 cut [5]. Weighted 7.96/12 = 6.63, rounded to 7; liquidity is ~$61M per day.

ai_resilience.label: LOW RISK
ai_resilience.analysis: AI Risk Protection (8/9): Harley's earnings come from building and selling physical heavyweight motorcycles through a dealer network and financing those purchases, an emotional, physical-world experience AI cannot substitute [1][3]. Its real risks are demographic demand, tariffs ($75-90M of expected 2026 cost) and consumer credit, not AI displacement [2]. AI Opportunity (0/1): No AI revenue.

infinite_game.summary: Harley-Davidson has one of the most enduring brand causes in American business, surviving more than 120 years of depressions, wars and near-bankruptcy. Recent leadership has swung from Jochen Zeitz's Hardwire/EV strategy to Starrs' 'Back to the Bricks', reversed DEI under boycott pressure, and sold a finance stake partly to fund $500M of shareholder returns. Sinek would see a strong cause served by short-cycle, reactive strategy.

just_cause.analysis: Just Cause (2/3): Freedom and the pursuit of adventure is a genuine, idealistic cause that has drawn a loyal community for generations; Starrs' team itself identified the name, loyal customers and dealers as Harley's lasting strengths [3]. Repeated strategic resets prevent the full 3 points.

trusting_teams.analysis: Trusting Teams (0/2): A 2025 CEO change from Zeitz to Starrs, a mandated return to the Juneau Avenue headquarters, a 2024 boycott-driven DEI reversal, and a 2025 activist proxy campaign against the board all point to organizational instability [3][4].

worthy_rivals.analysis: Worthy Rivals (0/1): No evidence was found of management framing competitors such as Indian, BMW or Royal Enfield as sources of learning; the strategy discussion centers on Harley's own brand and dealers [3].

existential_flexibility.analysis: Existential Flexibility (1/2): Spinning out LiveWire as a separately listed EV company was a real bet on the future of motorcycling, but Harley's core remains internal-combustion cruisers and the new strategy doubles down on them [2][3].

courage_to_lead.analysis: Courage to Lead (1/2): Management accepted an 8% shipment decline to cut dealer inventory 26% and restore dealer profitability, sacrificing near-term revenue for channel health [1]. However, about $500M of the HDFS proceeds was earmarked for shareholder returns [4].

investment_thesis: Harley's turnaround is gaining traction: Q3 2026 North American retail rose 9%, the fourth straight quarter of growth, while global dealer inventory fell 26%, and management raised HDMC and HDFS guidance for the second time in 2026 [1]. The $5B HDFS loan-book sale to KKR and PIMCO de-risked the balance sheet (D/E now 76.7%) and funded debt reduction and returns, and the stock offers a 2.4% yield with a 33-year payment record at 15.6x forward earnings [4][5].
thesis_continued: The bear case is structural: revenue has shrunk from $5.84B in 2023 to $4.47B in 2025 and fell another 19.2% YoY, TTM margins are negative, and July guidance called for only $10-50M of HDMC operating income with $75-90M of tariff costs [2][5]. LiveWire continues to lose $70-80M a year, the core rider base is aging, and the 2024 DEI boycott and leadership churn show brand and governance vulnerability [2][4].
key_catalysts: Continued North American retail growth (+9% in Q3 2026) from lower-priced Super Glide and Deadwood models
Dealer inventory normalization (-26% YoY) allowing shipments to re-align with retail in 2027
Strategic options for loss-making LiveWire ($70-80M 2026 operating loss guide)
key_risks: Tariff costs of $75-90M in 2026 compressing an already thin HDMC operating income guide of $10-50M
Aging core customer demographic and weak younger-rider adoption driving secular volume decline
Consumer credit deterioration affecting retained HDFS economics despite the KKR/PIMCO loan-book sale
